title: Letter 31 — On Rest and the Knowledge of Oneself
attribution_note: Letter 31 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: *“My friend and brother in Christ!”*
I thank you for the letter you sent us, and to yours I reply according to my strength.

sections.heading: That rest is not found in this age

pairs.en: 1. Truly you acknowledge that there is nothing more pleasant than tranquillity — this is the first blessedness in this world. Without rest nothing is pleasant to us. We know this in time of battle, when evil, fear and every confusion come upon us, even as we know how great a good health is when health is taken away. But rest in this age cannot be found. The sea is inconstant: it comes and it goes, and is almost always troubled — so also is our life. Man seeks rest and goes from place to place for its sake, yet nowhere finds it, for he seeks that which is not in this world. He withdraws from the bustle of life into the wilderness, but there greater and more cruel temptations meet us from thoughts and from the assaults of demons; in cities and villages we are surrounded by offences, which always touch and kindle our hearts. *“Woe unto the world because of offences!”* [Matthew 18:7]

sections.heading: The inner rest, the desired sabbath

pairs.en: 2. Christians, though outwardly they find no rest — for always either inward or outward things trouble them with temptations — yet inwardly they can and ought to have rest always and in every place. A good conscience, which is not reproved in evil deeds, words and thoughts, and a soul that overcomes all that is contrary, and has strengthened herself by patience, stands in rest as in a quiet harbour.

This is our blessedness in this age; this is the most desired sabbath-rest, which we must keep not only on one day of the week, but every day and hour. This sabbath our God requires of us. Let the Jews, the enemies of Christ's Cross, keep their sabbath; but we must hold to this sabbath and keep it firmly. The flesh, the world and the devil strive to destroy it in us; but we must with all our strength, with God's help, defend and preserve it. In this desired sabbath-rest *“righteousness and peace have kissed each other.”* [Psalm 84:11] This I desire for you and for myself from the heart.

sections.heading: Temptation as the means of self-knowledge

pairs.en: 3. We cannot know ourselves better than by temptation that befalls us from within and from without. Temptation shows us to ourselves — what we are, and what is hidden within us. Temptation, like a purging medicine, opens what our soul is sick with; as by a stroke the sound of a bell is known, and whether a newly made pot is strong, and by squeezing what air a bellows is filled with is known — so a man does not know himself until he is tried in various ways.

Many dream something of themselves before temptation; but having been tried they know what they are, and thereafter hold another opinion. I too had thought to withdraw from this place, but having considered, I remained and cast myself upon God's Providence, acknowledging that this is better for me, that I may know myself.

We have a simple proverb among all: “He who has been tried knows all.” And so there is no better means of knowing oneself than temptation. Thanks be to God, that He sends temptations upon us! Thus He brings us to the knowledge of ourselves, and to know oneself is the beginning of Christian blessedness. Therefore the more you endure temptation, the more you know yourself.

sections.heading: Scripture, and meditation upon the Creator

pairs.en: 4. The second means, or even the first, is meditation upon Holy Scripture, which sets before us the old man and the new with their works, that we may put off the first and put on the second [see Colossians 3:9–10]. All Holy Scripture presents these two. But here temptation is needful, for it reveals the old man living in us.

5. The third means is meditation upon the Creator and the creation, upon eternity and time, upon Christ and His incarnation. For what end were we born, and do we live in this world? Not for this age, but for the age to come are we born into this world; for our life in this world is nothing other than a continual journey toward the age to come. But this way is broad or narrow. The broad leads to destruction, and the narrow goes into everlasting life. The broad is called broad because the people, the travellers who go by it, live according to their own will, and do what they will; and the narrow is called narrow because those who go by it subject and captivate their will to the will of God, and it is straitened by the endurance of troubles, sorrows and every adversity.

Upon the strait way the new man goes, but from the strait way the old man draws us away. Here we must seek the new man, that we may be strengthened and not turned aside. And woe unto us, that we are inclined to evil: the flesh always *“lusteth against the Spirit”* [Galatians 5:17]. O God, set us and strengthen us upon this saving, narrow way, which draws into everlasting spaciousness, and draw us along it after Thee, that we may inherit rest!

6. Whence do we see that every place and every time is convenient for the knowledge of oneself? Because at every time and in every place temptation meets us, and always and everywhere we can think and meditate upon what has been written above.

7. You write truly, that time is precious, and nothing is more precious than it. Of all that is lost we can find something, but lost time cannot be recovered, as a word once spoken cannot be brought back. And this troubles me greatly. But let us strive at least not to lose that which remains, and to make good what has been lost with that by which it is made good. May God by His grace supply for those who repent and pray. O God, turn our mind to eternity!...

sections.heading: Counsel of solitude and holy reading

pairs.en: 8. For you, by reason of what has been written above, there is no more convenient place than a place of solitude, whither I counsel you to remove, and to begin from the beginning to read the holy Bible, with meditation upon the various works of God which it will set before you, and always — morning and night — to exercise yourself in it, and to read Arndt through, and into other books to walk as one goes visiting, and to sharpen mind and will unto the good, and to wait upon God's calling, whither and when God shall call you — and so you shall be at rest.
